content:
In my very first week, I realized some things would be harder than I expected. One in particular: the language.
I had studied English before — a few times, actually. But I’ll be honest: spending hours with a book in my hands was never really my thing. That’s exactly why I always liked IT. Most of what I know, I learned hands-on — by doing, breaking, fixing. Studying theory sitting still never worked for me the way practice does.
English was no different — except that, back in Brazil, “hands-on” English is rare. I had a decent base. I worked at a large company that had been acquired by an American multinational, so meetings with Americans and emails in English were part of my routine.
The problem is that a quick meeting, or an email, is nothing like living fully immersed in the language.
And that’s exactly what Canada taught me right away.
Simple things suddenly got a little harder. Going to the grocery store to buy anything, for example. There came the doubt: the label is different, the images are different, I actually had to read to understand what it was. And what did I find? Words I had never seen before.
Makes sense, right? Like I said, my English was meeting English. And it’s not hard to see that, in a war room, in the middle of an incident investigation, nobody is discussing the ingredients of some random canned food. My work vocabulary wasn’t saving me in the grocery aisle.
But that, I’ll admit, was actually the easy part. Phone in hand, ChatGPT open, I’d ask, translate, learn. And that’s how it went — one new food at a time, one new word at a time.
The real challenge came later. Guess what the second wall was? Accents.
It wasn’t my first time in Canada — but before, I’d come as a tourist, and tourism is a whole different thing. Living here, it hit me: the thing this country has the least of is Canadians. Europeans from everywhere, Indians, Africans, Iranians, Filipinos… my goodness, so many nationalities. And with them, so many levels of English, so many different accents, all at once.
I learned two things almost immediately.
The first: understanding people was going to be much harder than I imagined — not because of my English, but because everyone brought their own.
The second, and this one I carry to this day: we Brazilians worry way too much about our level of English. And the truth is, nobody — absolutely nobody — cares about it. In a country built by immigrants, everyone has an accent, everyone makes mistakes, and life goes on. The accent isn’t the problem we imagine it to be.
And that’s when I made a decision that, for someone who always ran from books, was almost ironic: I needed to study English again. Even the basics. Especially the basics.
Not to pass any test. But to handle real life — to learn the words I was missing, to understand the nuances I had only just started noticing now that I was living immersed in them. Practice had shown me, the hard way, exactly where I needed to go back to.
So I started. From the very beginning. From the verb to be. No shame, no rush — just starting over, like so many other things in my life at that moment.
And that’s what I want to share with you from here on: the basics I revisited, the ones that make all the difference for anyone just arriving. Let’s go.
Survival English: the verb to be If there’s one place to start over, it’s here. To be is the most basic and most used verb in English. It works as both “to exist” and “to be in a state or place,” and it’s the first step to building almost any sentence.
The three forms in the present:
Pronoun to be Example Meaning I am I am Brazilian. identity / who you are You / We / They are You are late. state / condition He / She / It is She is at SAIT. location / place One thing to know: unlike many languages that split this into two separate verbs, English uses to be for both who you are and how/where you are. “I am a security analyst” and “I am tired” use the exact same verb.
Contractions (everyone uses these in real life):
Nobody says “I am” all the time out on the street. In practice it becomes:
I am → I’m (I’m from Brazil.) You are → You’re (You’re right.) He is → He’s / She is → She’s (She’s my wife.) It is → It’s (It’s cold today.) ← you’ll use this one A LOT in Canada We are → We’re (We’re new here.) They are → They’re (They’re from India.) Negative — just add not:
I’m not ready. It’s not that cold. Questions — flip the order:
Are you okay? Is it far? Am I late? In real life, right after arriving, you’ll hear and use things like:
“I’m looking for work.” “It’s my first week here.” “Are you from around here?” “We’re new in Calgary.” Tip from someone who’s been there: don’t be afraid to mix up is/are/am. Even if you get it wrong, people understand. What matters is speaking. Remember: nobody is judging your English as much as you think.
But this is just the beginning. On top of brushing up on my English, I also needed to go after a job. And guess what? I found out that the résumé format in Canada is quite different from the one we use in Brazil. And LinkedIn? The way they see it here is a whole different story too.
But that’s a topic for the next post.

I had studied English before — a few times, actually. But I’ll be honest: spending hours with a book in my hands was never really my thing. That’s exactly why I always liked IT. Most of what I know, I learned hands-on — by doing, breaking, fixing. Studying theory sitting still never worked for me the way practice does.
title: Real-world English

content:
Before any suitcase, before the plane, before the Canadian cold, there was a different kind of cold — the knot in my stomach on the day I quit my job.
I had a stable job. Good salary, investments, money saved. On paper, everything people tell you not to walk away from. The severance was actually decent — even after losing part of it for resigning — and for a moment I felt a flash of joy. But it came bundled with the math I was already running in my head: that money was going to shrink, and I had nothing lined up on the other side.
I quit a week or two before the move. And they were the fullest weeks of my life. While I packed suitcases and tried to fit an entire life into a few kilos, I was also trying to be there for my family, who were going through a hard time. Starting over never comes at a clean moment. It comes in the middle of everything.
The knot in my stomach only got tighter.
On the day of the trip, we went to the airport with family. We talked, we put off the goodbye as long as we could. Then came the last hug. And then boarding.
The flight was calm. I talked with my wife until sleep got the better of her, and I sat there with my thoughts and the hum of the plane, crossing the ocean toward a life I still had no idea how to picture.
Our first landing was in Montreal — that’s where we’d clear immigration before continuing on to Calgary. When the plane touched the ground, we both looked out the window at the same time.
Snow.
It was the first time either of us had ever seen snow. Everything was white, as far as we could see. I remember it like it was yesterday: my wife turned to me and said — “Did we really just do this?” I laughed. “Yeah, we did. We’re here.”
The emotion lasted exactly until immigration.
First hurdle: we went to the wrong counter. The officer was not happy about it — almost annoyed, he told us this wasn’t the place, that we needed another section to sort out my wife’s study permit, since she’d be studying at SAIT, and my work permit — me, the one who’d be working. Or rather: looking for work.
We found the right section. And there, the complete opposite: the second officer was kind, handled everything, issued both permits without any drama. But the whole mix-up had cost us — we were now late for our connecting flight. To top it off, we left through the wrong door.
Then the running started. The two of us, carry-ons in hand, racing across the airport in search of the right gate. We made it just in time — the plane was waiting only for us, and the agent was already calling our names over the speaker. We stepped on board out of breath, a little embarrassed, a little relieved, and sank into our seats.
Next stop: Calgary. Our new home.
When the plane finally landed, we waited for our bags — some had been checked — and met the person who would take us to our apartment.
Outside, it was about -10°C. (Looking back now, I think that wasn’t even real cold. At the time, it felt absurd.) But honestly, in that moment the cold didn’t even matter — we were too excited. We’d made it. We were here.
We got to the apartment, started unpacking, and got ready to rest after a long journey full of emotion. A journey that had begun, weeks earlier, with a knot in my stomach on the day I quit — and ended there, on the other side of the world, in a new home, in a new country, with snow outside the window.
The leap had happened. Now it was time to live it.
(And that’s when the real challenges began — starting with English. But that’s for the next chapter.)

title: The arrival

content:
After more than 20 years working in technology and information security, I decided to change the course of my life. I left a stable job and moved to Canada — with nothing lined up on the other side, starting again almost from scratch.
It was a decision that brought together a long-held desire to live abroad and the right moment to finally act on it. And it came with challenges I knew existed on paper, but that feel very different once you’re actually living them: the language in everyday life, the financial uncertainty of starting over, and the full weight of an immigration process.
I created this blog to document that journey — the technical side, with procedures and lessons from my day-to-day work implementing and managing tools and infrastructure, and also the human side of moving to a new country and learning to live in another language.
If you’re thinking about taking a similar path, or you’re simply curious about what making this kind of leap is like, I hope you find something useful here. Welcome.
